extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, authors, and creative-writing students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and structuring 'scenes' and 'sequels' in fiction: how to make scenes advance plot and sequels process events and set new goals, plus how to balance them for pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene as a unit of conflict (goal → conflict → disaster)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene is a unit of conflict, an account of an effort to attain a goal despite opposition. Swain's structure of a scene is (1) goal, (2) conflict, (3) disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions of a scene: provide interest and advance the story. A scene should present a character attempting to achieve a specific goal, encounter opposition (conflict), and end in a setback or disaster that propels action or change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene continuity: unbroken flow of action
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene should have an unbroken flow of action without a lapse of time or leap from one setting to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain temporal and spatial continuity within a scene so the reader experiences it as a single unit of action; avoid jumps in time or setting that would fragment the scene's immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequel as transition (reaction → dilemma → decision) and its functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequel is a unit of transition that links two scenes; Swain describes its structure as (1) reaction, (2) dilemma, and (3) decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequel functions: translate disaster into a goal, telescope reality, and control tempo. Use sequels to let characters process what happened, weigh options (dilemma), and choose the next course of action (decision) that sets up the next scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive vs. reactive scene types
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than strictly separate 'scene' and 'sequel', some authors treat passages as proactive (character initiates action) or reactive (character responds to events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and write scenes according to whether the protagonist is driving events (proactive) or responding (reactive); both types are valid and often interlock within a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and pacing via proportion of scenes to sequels
rubrics_metrics.description: An author controls pacing with the proportion of scene to sequel; flexibility is important versus a mechanical approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust the ratio of active scenes to reflective sequels to produce peaks (scenes) and valleys (sequels) in narrative tempo. Avoid a formulaic pattern—use more or fewer sequels to control speed and reader rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomy of a scene (purpose, change, hooking beginning, rising tension, decisive ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before crafting a scene, its purpose relative to the story must be known; each scene must advance the plot and effect change in the character. Each scene should have a beginning (hook), middle (rising tension/conflict), and end (character processing and response that sets up the next scene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nothing new happens or the character is unchanged, the scene is ineffective. Scenes should respond to the previous passage: something happens (physically or emotionally), the character reacts/changes, then decides what to do next. The beginning must hook the reader; the middle must not lag; tension can be internal, interpersonal, or informational rather than purely action-packed; the scene should end with a reaction/decision that triggers the subsequent scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate classification of passages (scene, sequel, neither, both)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages may be scenes, sequels, passages that are neither (fragments, narration, description, exposition), or passages that include elements of both (e.g., problem-solving passages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a passage's function is to enact conflict (scene), process events (sequel), simply narrate/describe (neither), or combine both functions (both). Example: problem-solving passages common in mystery/detective stories blend scene/action and sequel/reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose scene type by position, dominant mode, and specialized role
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes can be classified by their position within the story (opening, climax), by the fiction-writing mode dominating them (action, dialogue), or by specialized roles (flashback, flashforward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the scene's form and focus to match its narrative role—an opening scene must hook and establish stakes; a climax scene must heighten conflict; an action scene emphasizes movement, while a dialogue scene emphasizes exchange and character. Use flashbacks/forwards when they serve a clear purpose.
